# Radial neuropathies

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Upper extremity > Radial neuropathies*

[Original Article Link](/library/_R05pf)

---

## Summary

Radial neuropathies are conditions caused by acute or chronic injury to the <u>radial nerve</u>. Clinical presentations vary with the mechanism, site, and extent of nerve injury. The <u>radial nerve</u> arises from the <u>posterior cord of the brachial plexus</u>, which comprises cervical roots C5–T1. Within the upper extremity, the <u>radial nerve</u> has <u>lateral</u> cutaneous sensory branches and innervates extensors. When injured, radial neuropathies are therefore characterized by sensory symptoms of <u>pain</u>, <u>paresthesia</u>, and numbness, as well as motor symptoms of <u>weakness</u> of extension at the <u>elbow</u>, wrist (“<u>wrist drop</u>”), and/or fingers. Several <u>risk factors</u> are associated with subtypes of radial neuropathies, including crutch use, intoxication, <u>fracture</u> of the <u>humerus</u> or radius, use of tight watch bands or handcuffs, and repetitive <u>pronation</u> and <u>supination</u>. The <u>patient history</u> and examination, including <u>Tinel's sign</u>, may be sufficient for diagnosis in some cases, but <u>x-ray</u> is necessary in the presence of trauma, and electrodiagnostics, though less useful than in <u>carpal tunnel syndrome</u>, may be considered if symptoms persist. <u>Conservative management</u>, consisting of local <u>corticosteroid</u> injections and counseling to reduce <u>risk factors</u>, is typically the treatment of choice in nontraumatic cases. Surgical decompression, with approach varying by location, may be considered in refractory cases.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Risk factors</u> vary according to the location of the injury:

* <u>Axilla</u>: improper crutch use (crutch palsy)

* Mid-arm:

* <u>Fracture</u> of <u>humerus</u> (<u>radial nerve</u> runs in <u>spiral groove</u>)

* Compression of the <u>radial nerve</u> due to draping of arm over furniture (saturday night palsy) or pressure on the <u>axilla</u> or upper <u>medial</u> arm; more likely in the setting of intoxication, anesthesia, or <u>sleep</u> (<u>honeymoon palsy</u>)

* <u>Elbow</u>: radial tunnel syndrome (controversial diagnosis ) due to chronic compression within the <u>radial tunnel</u>

* Deep forearm: posterior interosseous nerve syndrome (a syndrome characterized by <u>weakness</u> of muscles in the <u>extensor compartment of the forearm</u>) due to <u>fracture</u> of the <u>radial head</u> or chronic <u>soft tissue</u> compression

* <u>Superficial</u> forearm or wrist: <u>superficial</u> <u>radial nerve</u> compression, called “cheiralgia paresthetica,” often due to tight wristwatches or handcuffs or repetitive <u>pronation</u> and <u>supination</u>

## Clinical features

| Site of lesion | Sensory symptoms | Motor symptoms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Axilla</u> | <br>* All below<br><br> | <br><br>* All below<br><br>* <u>Paralysis</u> of the <u>triceps</u> muscle may occur if the <u>radial nerve</u> is injured in the <u>axilla</u>.<br><br><br> |
| Mid-arm | <br><br>* All below<br><br>* Numbness, <u>paresthesia</u>, <u>pain</u> along <u>lateral</u> <u>posterior</u> arm<br><br><br> | <br><br>* All below<br><br>* Wrist drop<br><br>* <u>Paralysis</u> or <u>weakness</u> of the hand and finger extensors, which results in decreased grip strength (wrist extension ensures the optimal action of finger flexors)<br><br>* The patient cannot extend their hand at the <u>wrist joint</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Elbow</u> (<u>radial tunnel</u>) | <br>* <u>Pain</u> and tenderness following extension or repetitive <u>pronation</u>/<u>supination</u> [[1]](/library/Ela8Ak)<br><br> | <br>* Sometimes <u>weakness</u> of extension and <u>supination</u>, secondary to <u>pain</u> (not to missing innervation!)<br><br> |
| Deep forearm (<u>proximal</u> <u>posterior interosseous nerve</u>) | <br>* None [[2]](/library/mlaVxk)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Paralysis</u> of the finger extensors (no true <u>wrist drop</u>)<br><br> |
| <u>Superficial</u> forearm and wrist (<u>superficial</u> <u>radial nerve</u>) | <br>* Deficits on the radial side of the dorsum of the hand (thumb, index finger, and the radial half of the middle finger)  [[3]](/library/Llawxk)<br><br> | <br>* None<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> The higher (more <u>proximal</u>) the lesion, the greater the number of extensor muscles involved!

## Treatment

* The treatment of choice depends on the severity and persistence of symptoms.

* <u>Conservative therapy</u>

* Rest

* <u>NSAIDs</u>

* Local <u>glucocorticoid</u> injections (if needed)

* <u>Physical therapy</u>

* Surgical therapy in severe and treatment-resistant cases: nerve decompression, <u>neurorrhaphy</u>, nerve <u>transplantation</u>, <u>tendon</u> transfer [[6]](/library/MlaMxk)

* Orthopedic repair of <u>fractures</u>, <u>dislocations</u>, or other traumatic injuries
